content: When screening registries are available, such as in prisons or among pregnant women with multiple antenatal care visits, it is essential to utilize these resources effectively. Regular and repeated biomarker surveys should be conducted to monitor the prevalence of hepatitis B and C. Sentinel surveillance sites are critical for estimating the proportion of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and decompensated cirrhosis cases attributable to hepatitis B and C. Mortality data should be obtained from death registries to understand the broader impact of these diseases. Populations presenting with acute hepatitis symptoms in healthcare facilities, as well as asymptomatic individuals tested during population surveys, should be included in surveillance efforts. Additionally, individuals diagnosed with cirrhosis or HCC should be monitored. Case definitions must be clearly established, including presumptive and confirmed cases of acute hepatitis (by type), chronic hepatitis B and C, serological evidence of past or present HCV infection, cases of HCC or decompensated cirrhosis, and HDV coinfection among those with HBV infection. Communicable disease surveillance systems, whether nationwide or sentinel-based, should be implemented in coordination with hepatitis programs and other stakeholders conducting biomarker surveys. Vital registration systems, sentinel sites caring for individuals with decompensated cirrhosis and HCC, and cancer registries should also be leveraged. Existing guidelines and protocols, such as standard operating procedures for enhanced reporting of acute hepatitis cases and templates for biomarker prevalence surveys, should be adapted and utilized at the country level. In the event of an outbreak, in vitro diagnostic testing should be organized on a sample of cases to ensure accurate identification. High-quality data from a smaller number of tertiary centers is preferable to low-quality data from numerous sites, as it ensures reliability and efficiency. Consolidated guidelines on person-centered viral hepatitis strategic information should be used to support the scale-up of prevention, diagnosis, and treatment services at the country level. A strategic information framework should prioritize key indicators to monitor the health sector's response to chronic hepatitis B and C. This framework should help countries systematically collect and analyze data to guide their health sector strategies. Indicators should be organized by priority and linked in a results chain to support high-quality care across the health sector cascade for chronic viral hepatitis services. The framework builds on globally and regionally established conceptual and monitoring frameworks for health system strengthening, primary healthcare, and universal health coverage. Indicators should be categorized into core, global, and additional groups. Core indicators are feasible to collect and monitor in most contexts, while global indicators are a subset of core indicators relevant for global monitoring and reporting to the World Health Assembly. Additional indicators are desirable but may not be feasible in all contexts. Countries are encouraged to select and adapt a parsimonious set of indicators based on their specific context, priorities, and health system maturity. Indicators should be balanced across the results chain and conceptual framework domains, with a focus on high-priority areas. Data disaggregation is critical for identifying and addressing inequalities. Viral hepatitis data should be disaggregated by age, sex, high-risk population groups, geographical location, pregnancy status, coinfection status, and facility type. This approach ensures that services reach those in need equitably and that no one is left behind in efforts to eliminate viral hepatitis. Disaggregated data also enable comparisons between public and private sector performance, which is particularly important in countries where the private sector delivers substantial chronic viral hepatitis care and treatment. The monitoring and evaluation framework for viral hepatitis B and C should align with global health sector strategies and national accountability frameworks. Regular multistakeholder reviews of strategy implementation should be conducted at the national level, with strong civil society participation and transparent assessment and reporting. These reviews should identify bottlenecks and improve the overall quality of the programmatic response. The results chain provides a structure for analysis and facilitates alignment with country data systems. Disaggregated data and person-centered monitoring are essential for improving the monitoring and evaluation of hepatitis programs. Joint efforts to strengthen health information systems should lead to better data collection, analysis, and use, ultimately supporting evidence-informed decision-making and accountability.
